prompt:
Feature: enforce the route permission helpers in the route modules (semgrep in CI), starting with the invitation routes.

Routes declare the permission they need with require(Perm.X), checked by RequirePermission, and tests/integration_tests/test_route_permissions.py keeps the table of every route that declares one. Two handlers were left behind: creating an invite token (POST /api/households/invitations) and emailing an invitation (POST /api/households/invitations/email) still test the user's can_invite flag inside the handler. They are missing from the table, and because a handler only runs after FastAPI has validated the request body, a user without can_invite who sends an incomplete body (for example {}) gets a 422 validation error instead of 403.

Expected:
1. Both routes declare Perm.GROUP_INVITE the way the other guarded routes declare theirs: a RequirePermission(Perm.GROUP_INVITE) among the route's own direct dependencies, which is what shows up on `route.dependant.dependencies` when walking `fastapi.routing.iter_route_contexts(app.routes)`, as the table test does. The in-handler can_invite checks go away.
2. A user of the same household with every permission flag off (canInvite, canManage, canManageHousehold and canOrganize false, not an admin) gets 403 from both routes whatever the body, including an empty JSON object {}: the permission is checked before the body is validated. A user with can_invite is not refused (an empty body then gets the usual 422, and a valid request works as before). The other checks in these handlers stay as they are: the 403 when password login is disabled, and the admin-only rule for tokens for another group or household. GET /api/households/invitations (admins only) keeps its own check and declares no permission.
3. The declared table is the one already in tests/integration_tests/test_route_permissions.py plus a new GROUP_INVITE entry with exactly POST /api/households/invitations and POST /api/households/invitations/email. No other route gains or loses a declaration. Add the new entry to that table.

The project also wants this kept that way by semgrep rules run in CI over the route modules: no handler branching on a can_organize, can_manage, can_manage_household or can_invite flag (declare the permission instead), and no hand-built HTTPException for 403 or 404 (raise the forbidden() and not_found() helpers from the module that holds Perm, each taking an optional message). semgrep is not installed in the project environment, so that lint and its CI step are optional here. If you move other routes' 403 and 404 errors onto the helpers, keep each response's status code and body as they are now.

Tests: `python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/integration_tests/test_route_permissions.py tests/integration_tests/user_household_tests` for quick loops; the whole backend suite is `python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests` (about 8 minutes).
title: feat: enforce route permission helpers with semgrep in CI (#8769)
